paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to make learning a new task possible with little task-specific data. Evaluating that ability becomes harder when training tasks are very diverse or when new tasks differ from those encountered during training. Standard benchmarks often make these conditions difficult to isolate because researchers cannot easily measure or adjust the distributions from which tasks come.

This paper proposes channel coding as a setting where those distributions can be controlled. It is also a practical application in which quickly adapting to new tasks is valuable. The benchmark lets researchers vary both how broadly training tasks differ and how much the test tasks depart from the training distribution, making these factors explicit parts of evaluation.

The authors use the benchmark to study how task diversity and distribution shift affect meta-learning performance. Its contribution is a way to investigate these challenges systematically within an application that motivates adaptation. This creates a basis for assessing where meta-learning works reliably and for developing methods that remain effective under broader or changing task conditions.
neurips-2021-a-channel-coding-benchmark-.tldr: A channel coding benchmark makes task diversity and distribution shift controllable for studying meta-learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning studies how neural networks can keep learning as incoming data changes, while reducing interference with what they learned previously. Comparing methods is difficult when each study constructs its own sequence of tasks. The paper identifies a particular weakness in existing evaluations: they often divide and concatenate static vision datasets to imitate a changing stream.

The authors introduce a computer graphics framework that continually generates an urban world. It renders the fragments of the scene that are coming next, supporting an endless process that runs in real time. A modular generative model controls the world through adjustable parameters, so researchers can compose streams by changing the factors responsible for the generated data.

This design makes the construction of changing data streams part of the experimental framework itself. Researchers can use adjustable generative factors to investigate continual learning schemes in a more systematic way. The contribution is an evaluation resource that supports detailed analysis of learning under changing conditions, addressing the difficulty of comparing methods through separately assembled static benchmarks.
neurips-2021-a-procedural-world-generati.tldr: A controllable urban-world simulator generates changing visual data streams for systematic continual learning evaluation.

paragraphs: Building a hate speech dataset involves both finding relevant examples and deciding how to label them. Randomly sampled tweets contain relatively little hate speech, but collecting only tweets with predefined hate words can miss other forms. Annotation introduces another challenge: people bring different interpretations of hate speech and may struggle to apply shared guidelines consistently.

The paper connects these difficulties to information retrieval, where relevant material can also be rare and judgments subjective. It uses pooling and active learning to select tweets for annotation more efficiently. It also breaks annotation into component tasks and collects annotators' rationales, aiming to make decisions more consistent and useful beyond the final labels.

The resulting Twitter benchmark covers broader forms of hate than earlier datasets. Existing detection models suffer a dramatic accuracy drop on that broader coverage, showing that their performance depends strongly on which examples evaluation includes. The collected rationales explain labeling decisions and could support future models trained with explanations or designed to generate them.
neurips-2021-an-information-retrieval-ap.tldr: Information retrieval methods produce a broader hate speech benchmark that exposes substantial weaknesses in existing detectors.

paragraphs: A single overall score can hide substantial differences in how a language model handles different kinds of examples. Test sets sampled from the overall data distribution emphasize common cases, leaving rare language phenomena and text about underrepresented groups less visible. The paper argues that this evaluation pattern can encourage models to fit the most frequent parts of the data.

The authors develop a framework for automatically constructing more targeted evaluations. It can identify subsets of existing data and create controlled changes to examples. The framework accommodates tasks that map text to a scalar value, text to other text, or structured data to text, giving the challenge-set approach a scope beyond one particular generation task.

Applied to the GEM generation benchmark, the framework produces 80 challenge sets. These support analyses of specific model capabilities and reveal limits of the evaluated generation models. The contribution is a practical way to supplement aggregate performance with focused tests, making it easier to examine which portions of a task a model handles well.
neurips-2021-automatic-construction-of-e.tldr: An automated framework creates 80 GEM challenge sets to reveal model behavior hidden by aggregate evaluation scores.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning usually depends on a reward function that expresses what behavior is desirable. Designing that function can be difficult for complex tasks. Preference-based learning offers another route: an agent learns using a teacher's judgments about preferred behavior. B-Pref addresses the lack of a common benchmark for comparing methods that learn this way.

The central evaluation problem is how to represent the teacher. Repeatedly collecting real human feedback makes quick algorithm comparisons impractical, while a simulated teacher that always agrees perfectly with the underlying reward is unrealistic. B-Pref therefore simulates teachers with a range of irrationalities and evaluates robustness to those behaviors alongside task performance.

The authors use the benchmark to examine design choices in existing preference-based reinforcement learning algorithms, including how they select informative questions for a teacher. This makes feedback quality part of the evaluation rather than treating it as perfect by default. B-Pref provides a shared starting point for studying how learning methods respond when their preference signals are imperfect.
neurips-2021-b-pref-benchmarking-prefere.tldr: B-Pref evaluates preference-based reinforcement learning with simulated imperfect teachers and measures both performance and robustness.

paragraphs: Brax is an open-source, differentiable physics engine for simulating rigid bodies. Its design emphasizes performance and running many simulations in parallel on accelerators. Written in JAX, it provides a simulation foundation for reinforcement learning tasks, where a policy repeatedly acts in an environment and learns from the resulting experience.

The paper pairs the engine with JAX implementations of PPO, SAC, ES, and direct policy optimization. These learning algorithms compile alongside the simulated environments, allowing both learning and environment processing to happen on the same device. This integration matters because scaling a training system involves the interaction between its simulation and learning components, and Brax brings both into a shared accelerator-based setup.

The authors present results on tasks inspired by reinforcement learning literature and recreated in Brax. They also supply notebooks that support training performant policies on common MuJoCo-like tasks in minutes. The contribution combines a simulation library, compatible learning implementations, and runnable training examples, making the engine's emphasis on parallel execution accessible through complete learning workflows.
neurips-2021-brax-a-differentiable-physi.tldr: Brax combines accelerator-friendly rigid-body simulation with learning algorithms that run alongside environments on the same device.

paragraphs: Chaotic dynamical systems offer a useful combination for evaluating learning methods: their behavior challenges forecasting, while known mathematical properties make the source of the data interpretable. The paper builds a database of 131 such systems, each accompanied by precomputed time series containing either one measured variable or several.

Unlike a fixed collection of recordings, the underlying systems can be simulated again to generate additional sequences of arbitrary length and granularity. Each system also has annotations describing known mathematical properties. The authors analyze features of the generated data to categorize the different kinds of dynamics represented, connecting dataset diversity to properties of the systems producing it.

Across forecasting benchmarks, the paper relates prediction performance to the degree of chaos present. It also uses the data-generating systems in proof-of-concept studies involving transfer learning for time series classification, importance sampling to accelerate training, and symbolic regression evaluation. Together, these uses show how a benchmark with known, reusable generators can support both performance comparisons and investigation of what makes a task difficult.
neurips-2021-chaos-as-an-interpretable-b.tldr: A database of 131 chaotic systems provides regenerable time series and mathematical context for interpreting learning performance.

paragraphs: Unsupervised multi-object segmentation aims to separate a scene into individual objects without dense training annotations. Many methods had shown strong results on simple images with uniformly colored objects and plain backgrounds. ClevrTex tests whether that progress carries over to scenes with varied textures, materials, shapes, and more complicated lighting effects.

The dataset uses physically based rendering to create synthetic scenes containing three to ten objects. Its main collection has 50,000 examples built from 60 materials, with another 10,000 test images using 25 different materials. The authors also construct variants that control different aspects of scene complexity, allowing them to examine particular difficulties rather than treating complexity as one undifferentiated property.

In the reported benchmark, all evaluated state-of-the-art approaches fail to learn good representations in the textured setting despite impressive results on simpler data. This finding identifies a substantial gap between success on visually simple scenes and handling richer appearance. ClevrTex provides both a harder comparison task and controlled variants for probing the weaknesses behind that gap.
neurips-2021-clevrtex-a-texture-rich-ben.tldr: ClevrTex shows that strong unsupervised object segmentation results on simple scenes do not carry over to its textured scenes.

paragraphs: COVID-19 Sounds provides a shared dataset for studying whether respiratory audio can support machine learning screening. The work responds to concerns about limited data, transparency, and reproducibility in earlier efforts. It collects breathing, cough, and voice recordings through an app, making several types of respiratory sound available within one resource.

The release contains 53,449 audio samples totaling more than 552 hours, contributed by 36,116 participants. It covers varied demographics and health conditions and includes participants' self-reported COVID-19 testing status, with 2,106 samples associated with positive tests. That self-reported status is part of how the dataset describes the relationship between recordings and COVID-19.

The authors benchmark respiratory symptom prediction and COVID-19 prediction, reporting ROC-AUC values above 0.7 for these tasks. These results support the promise of the audio-based approach and the dataset's usefulness for research. The paper also describes an experimental setting intended to support fair future evaluation, positioning the release as a basis for reproducible comparisons and further respiratory health studies.
neurips-2021-covid-19-sounds-a-large-sca.tldr: COVID-19 Sounds releases respiratory recordings and benchmarks that support further study of audio-based health prediction.

paragraphs: Deepfake impersonation can involve both a person's appearance and their voice. A detector intended to examine these signals together needs data that includes both forms of manipulation. FakeAVCeleb addresses a gap in existing datasets, which the paper describes as focusing on either fake video or fake audio and also exhibiting racial bias.

The authors build a dataset containing manipulated videos paired with synthesized fake speech that is synchronized with lip movements. They use popular deepfake generation methods and source real celebrity videos from YouTube. The selected celebrities represent four ethnic backgrounds, an effort to address racial bias while creating data for a more realistic multimodal detection setting.

Experiments with state-of-the-art detection methods demonstrate the dataset's usefulness and the challenges it presents. The contribution gives researchers examples in which audio and visual manipulation can be studied collectively. Its demographic selection is a stated part of the dataset design, while the reported experiments establish a basis for evaluating detectors on this combined audio-video problem.
neurips-2021-fakeavceleb-a-novel-audio-v.tldr: FakeAVCeleb pairs deepfake videos with lip-synchronized synthetic audio to support multimodal detection research.

paragraphs: Synthetic images can differ from camera images even when they depict a virtual replica of the same scene. That mismatch complicates using simulation to develop 3D reconstruction algorithms. This paper addresses the issue by designing structured-light scanning hardware and its rendering pipeline together, explicitly connecting the physical acquisition system with the simulation.

On geometrically complex calibration objects with known material properties, the authors achieve negligible differences between real and synthesized images at the pixel level. This stated setting matters: the close agreement is demonstrated on those calibration objects. The approach supports generating large amounts of synthetic data using a system whose real and simulated outputs closely match under the described conditions.

The authors propose three benchmarks combining acquired and synthetic data: removing scanning noise, completing missing shape data, and reconstructing surfaces from dense point clouds. They also release high-resolution scans so researchers can use the system and benchmarks without rebuilding the hardware. The contribution joins acquisition design, simulation fidelity, and evaluation resources around several distinct stages of 3D reconstruction.
neurips-2021-hardware-design-and-accurat.tldr: Jointly designed scanning hardware and simulation closely match calibration images and support three 3D reconstruction benchmarks.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization searches for settings that make a learning algorithm work well on a dataset. Evaluating those settings can require substantial computation, motivating methods that reuse experience from earlier optimization tasks. Comparing such methods is difficult when studies choose different small collections of datasets and follow inconsistent experimental procedures.

HPO-B supplies a shared collection assembled and preprocessed from OpenML. It contains 6.4 million hyperparameter evaluations across 176 algorithm search spaces and 196 datasets. The evaluations cover these combinations sparsely, so the collection represents a large body of measured configurations without claiming that every possible combination has been evaluated.

The paper also specifies experimental protocols, data splits, and evaluation measures. These support comparisons both for methods that transfer information across tasks and for methods that optimize without such transfer. The contribution is therefore more than a large store of evaluation results: it pairs those results with common rules for using them, aiming to make black-box hyperparameter optimization comparisons faster, fairer, and reproducible.
neurips-2021-hpo-b-a-large-scale-reprodu.tldr: HPO-B combines 6.4 million hyperparameter evaluations with explicit protocols for reproducible optimization comparisons.

paragraphs: Answering questions about an abstract diagram requires more than recognizing objects in a natural photograph. IconQA targets this setting with problems inspired by real-world diagram word questions. Solving them can require reading text and recognizing icons alongside geometric, arithmetic, and commonsense reasoning, bringing perception and several reasoning skills into the same task.

The dataset contains 107,439 questions across three formats: choosing among images, choosing among text answers, and filling in a blank. The authors also release Icon645, a collection of 645,687 colored icons spanning 377 classes. This additional resource is intended to help models learn representations of the visual symbols used in icon-based questions.

The paper evaluates existing advanced visual question answering methods and includes user studies and blind experiments. It also introduces Patch-TRM, a baseline using a pyramid cross-modal Transformer with diagram embeddings pretrained on the icon dataset. Together, the question benchmark, icon resource, and baseline create a concrete setup for studying how models combine diagram interpretation with language-based reasoning.
neurips-2021-iconqa-a-new-benchmark-for-.tldr: IconQA benchmarks reasoning over icon diagrams and supplies a large icon dataset plus a dedicated Transformer baseline.

paragraphs: Learning to manipulate objects from 3D visual input requires coping with variation among objects of the same class. ManiSkill addresses a weakness in existing benchmarks: their assets often lack the geometric and topological diversity found within real-world object categories. It provides diverse objects in a full-physics simulator, with tasks selected to cover different manipulation challenges.

A moving panoramic camera supplies observations as point clouds or RGB-D images from the agent's perspective. This makes the benchmark suitable for studying policies that work from 3D visual information. Its combination of varied object shapes and visual observations connects the manipulation challenge directly to learning useful representations of the objects being handled.

ManiSkill supports learning through interaction and learning from demonstrations. The release includes approximately 36,000 successful trajectories and 1.5 million point-cloud or RGB-D frames, alongside baselines using 3D deep learning and demonstration-based methods. By providing the simulator, environments, software tools, and baselines, the authors create a shared resource for investigating generalizable manipulation across diverse objects.
neurips-2021-maniskill-generalizable-man.tldr: ManiSkill benchmarks visually guided manipulation across diverse objects and supplies about 36,000 successful demonstrations.

paragraphs: Diet planning involves both nutritional requirements and less explicit judgments about how foods should be composed into a diet. The MIND dataset addresses the need for data at this complete-diet level. Its creation process combines professional input with computational methods so that generating diets accounts for more than numerical nutrient targets alone.

Experts contribute knowledge about implicit composition requirements, while an operations research model specifies and applies explicit requirements. A controllable generative model automates diet generation within this combined approach. The resulting Korean Menus–Ingredients–Nutrients–Diets dataset includes 1,500 South Korean daily diets, 3,238 menus, and 3,036 ingredients, and considers recommended daily intake for 14 major nutrients.

The authors provide access and analysis through the Python package dietkit. They expect the resource to support machine learning research in diet planning and dietary healthcare. They also propose the combination of expert input, optimization, and controlled generation as a promising approach for creating synthetic data for other professional tasks, presenting that broader impact as an expectation.
neurips-2021-mind-dataset-for-diet-plann.tldr: MIND combines expert judgment, optimization, and controlled generation to create a dataset of nutritionally informed South Korean diets.

paragraphs: Tiny machine learning targets systems with extremely low power requirements. Assessing these systems involves more than asking whether a model predicts correctly: the time and energy needed to produce predictions also matter. MLPerf Tiny introduces a common benchmark suite intended to make those tradeoffs visible and comparisons reproducible across different systems.

The suite measures inference accuracy, latency, and energy. It includes four tasks: keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, and anomaly detection. Measuring several aspects of performance across these tasks gives submitters a shared basis for showing how their systems handle machine learning workloads under the constraints that motivate TinyML.

Developed through collaboration among more than 50 industry and academic organizations, the suite uses a modular design. That structure is intended to let contributors demonstrate improvements at different points in the deployment stack while maintaining fair comparison. The paper's central contribution is shared evaluation infrastructure that captures competing system requirements, supporting clearer assessment of progress in ultra-low-power machine learning.
neurips-2021-mlperf-tiny-benchmark-3bcae.tldr: MLPerf Tiny standardizes accuracy, latency, and energy evaluation across four ultra-low-power machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Human mathematical writing combines ordinary language with symbols. NaturalProofs provides a corpus of mathematical statements and proofs written in that form, supporting research on systems that understand mathematics as people express it. The collection spans multiple domains and combines sources with broad coverage, detailed coverage, and relatively limited available material.

The benchmark focuses on identifying key mathematical results used in proofs. It includes reference retrieval and generation tasks, testing whether a model can determine which results belong in a proof's supporting material. Its range of sources also enables evaluation within familiar distributions and zero-shot evaluation when generalizing to new settings.

The authors compare strong neural approaches with classical information retrieval methods. Large sequence models show promise, but their overall performance and generalization beyond the training domain still leave substantial room for improvement. These findings establish reference identification as a meaningful challenge for mathematical language models. The dataset supplies a basis for that evaluation and for further research involving naturally written mathematical statements and proofs.
neurips-2021-naturalproofs-mathematical-.tldr: NaturalProofs benchmarks identifying supporting mathematical results in human-written proofs and reveals substantial generalization challenges.

paragraphs: Graph learning methods must be both effective and computationally practical to work on very large scientific and industrial datasets. OGB-LSC addresses the shortage of public benchmarks at this scale. It provides three real-world datasets that are orders of magnitude larger than existing ones and cover link prediction, graph regression, and node classification.

The authors run baseline experiments that scale expressive graph models to these datasets. Those models significantly outperform simpler scalable baselines in the reported experiments. This finding shows that the benchmark's size does not eliminate the value of richer modeling and points to opportunities for improving the combination of predictive capability and large-scale execution.

The datasets also supported the ACM KDD Cup 2021, which attracted more than 500 team registrations and produced significant performance improvements through varied techniques. The paper summarizes common approaches among winning solutions and describes subsequent dataset updates. Its contribution combines demanding public tasks, baseline implementations, and experience from a large competition to support continued research on graph learning at scale.
neurips-2021-ogb-lsc-a-large-scale-chall.tldr: OGB-LSC provides three massive graph benchmarks where expressive models outperform simple scalable baselines.

paragraphs: Physion evaluates whether models can predict how a physical scene will change over time. Its realistic simulations include rigid and soft-body collisions, stable arrangements of several objects, rolling, sliding, and projectile motion. This range creates a broad test of physical prediction rather than restricting evaluation to one kind of event.

The authors compare models with different architectures, training objectives, input-output structures, and training data. They also measure human predictions on the same scenarios, enabling comparison of both performance and behavioral similarity. Vision models that represent individual objects generally do better than those that do not, but still remain far below human performance.

Graph neural networks given direct access to physical state information perform substantially better and make predictions more like people's. The results suggest that extracting useful physical representations from images is the main bottleneck for the evaluated vision approaches. The released data and code support reproducible comparisons, allowing future models to be assessed against the same physical scenarios and human judgments.
neurips-2021-physion-evaluating-physical.tldr: Physion suggests that extracting physical scene representations is a major bottleneck in human-like prediction from vision.

paragraphs: Few-shot text classification asks a model to learn a categorization task from only a small number of examples. RAFT focuses on whether progress in this ability translates into useful work on naturally occurring tasks. Its motivation is practical: existing benchmarks do not directly establish how well models can handle classification work previously performed by human research assistants.

The benchmark uses an evaluation setup intended to resemble deployment. Baseline results identify long texts and tasks with many possible classes as difficult areas for current techniques. These challenges help distinguish practical task demands from a broad impression that a model can learn effectively whenever a few labeled examples are available.

Human evaluations add another reference point. Some tasks are difficult even for non-experts, indicating that useful performance can depend on domain knowledge. Nevertheless, the non-expert human baselines exceed GPT-3 by an average of 0.11 in F1 score. RAFT's datasets and leaderboard provide a way to track whether model improvements reduce these applied gaps.
neurips-2021-raft-a-real-world-few-shot-.tldr: RAFT tests practical few-shot text classification and finds persistent gaps involving long texts, many classes, and human performance.

paragraphs: Paired images and text can train models to connect visual content with language. Collecting these pairs through search engines or web alt-text often introduces noise that requires extensive filtering. RedCaps explores Reddit as another source, aiming to obtain useful image-caption data with relatively little filtering while retaining a broad variety of objects and scenes.

The dataset contains 12 million image-text pairs gathered from a manually selected collection of subreddits. Choosing communities lets the authors influence the composition of the dataset without labeling each example individually. Those communities also supply coarse image labels, making the organization of the source platform part of the data collection strategy.

Captioning models trained on RedCaps generate rich, varied descriptions that humans prefer in the reported evaluation. They also learn visual representations that transfer to many downstream tasks. These results support the usefulness of community-curated image and text as training material, connecting the collection strategy to both language generation and reusable visual features.
neurips-2021-redcaps-web-curated-image-t.tldr: RedCaps collects 12 million Reddit image-text pairs that support human-preferred captions and transferable visual representations.

paragraphs: Time series outlier detection has many proposed algorithms, but comparing them depends on what counts as an outlier and how test data is constructed. The paper identifies ambiguity in existing definitions and substantial variation in synthetic data generation across applications. These differences make a shared basis for evaluation especially important.

The authors propose a behavior-based taxonomy that separates point-level outliers from pattern-level outliers and explicitly defines their context. They use this taxonomy to establish a general criterion for synthetic data generation, producing 35 datasets. They also select four multivariate real-world datasets from different domains, extending the comparison beyond generated examples.

Nine algorithms are evaluated across the synthetic and real-world collections. Some classical methods can outperform many recent deep learning approaches in these experiments, challenging an assumption that newer model families necessarily provide stronger results. The release includes datasets, preprocessing and generation scripts, and algorithm implementations, linking clearer task definitions with a reproducible way to investigate which methods work under different outlier conditions.
neurips-2021-revisiting-time-series-outl.tldr: A clearer outlier taxonomy and shared benchmark reveal cases where classical methods outperform recent deep learning approaches.

paragraphs: Segmentation models are usually trained to recognize a fixed set of categories, leaving them poorly equipped for unfamiliar objects. In automated driving, locating an unexpected object can matter even when the system cannot name it. SegmentMeIfYouCan supplies a benchmark for evaluating this problem and the related problem of finding obstacles on the road.

The benchmark distinguishes two tasks. Anomalous object segmentation concerns previously unseen categories, while road obstacle segmentation includes any object on the road, whether its category is familiar or unfamiliar. Two corresponding datasets come with an evaluation suite that combines established pixel-level measures with component-level measures that are insensitive to object size.

The authors evaluate multiple state-of-the-art baselines, including methods designed specifically for anomaly or obstacle segmentation, on both their datasets and public datasets. The results show that the new collections add diversity and difficulty to these evaluation settings. The explicit task distinction and complementary metrics support a more detailed assessment of how methods localize unusual objects and road hazards.
neurips-2021-segmentmeifyoucan-a-benchma.tldr: SegmentMeIfYouCan provides datasets and complementary metrics for unfamiliar-object segmentation and road-obstacle detection.

paragraphs: The brain's blood vessels form a spatial network closely connected to the organization of its neurons. Studying that network matters because changes in vessel structure can be early signs of conditions such as Alzheimer's disease or stroke. Advances in tissue clearing make it possible to image and segment the vasculature throughout a mouse brain.

Building on these imaging capabilities, the authors create an extensible dataset of whole-brain vessel graphs. They refine graph extraction using the Voreen volume rendering engine and make the resulting data available through OGB and PyTorch Geometric loaders. This connects specialized biological imaging outputs with tools used for developing and evaluating graph learning methods.

The paper benchmarks numerous graph algorithms on vessel prediction and vessel classification. The resource also raises challenges involving sparse spatial graphs with millions of nodes and edges, and how to incorporate biological prior knowledge into learning. Its contribution establishes a practical meeting point between neuroscience questions and graph learning methods that must handle very large, spatially organized structures.
neurips-2021-whole-brain-vessel-graphs-a.tldr: Whole-brain vessel graphs connect neuroscience tasks with graph learning challenges involving millions of spatially organized nodes and edges.

paragraphs: WikiChurches introduces architectural style classification using 9,485 images of church buildings, with both photographs and labels sourced from Wikipedia. The task requires distinguishing categories through subtle visual features. This makes the dataset relevant to fine-grained recognition, where identifying the broad kind of object does not resolve the more detailed classification question.

Several practical difficulties occur together in the collection. The sample size is comparatively small, classes are highly imbalanced, and photographs show buildings from widely varying viewpoints. Labels also form a hierarchy, with only some images labeled at the most specific level. Evaluation therefore involves both visual variation and uneven amounts and precision of supervision.

The authors additionally provide 631 bounding boxes marking characteristic visual features for 139 churches across four major categories. These annotations could support research that uses expert knowledge about distinctive object parts. Together, the image collection, hierarchical labels, and selected feature annotations offer a benchmark for investigating fine-grained classification under several challenges found in real-world data.
neurips-2021-wikichurches-a-fine-grained.tldr: WikiChurches tests architectural style recognition with subtle visual distinctions, imbalanced classes, varied viewpoints, and partially specific labels.
